information_for_contributors: Fenced-code injection: gives the fences md renders specially their own
language inside a Markdown document. Injected into `text.html.markdown`
by package.json, which also maps four of the `meta.embedded.block.*`
scopes below onto real language ids.
The shape of each rule is copied deliberately from VS Code's own
markdown-basics grammar (`fenced_code_block_css` and friends), down to the
`((\s+|:|,|\{|\?)[^`]*)?$` tail on the info string and the
`(^|\G)(\2|\s{0,3})(\3)\s*$` closing fence. Two reasons:
* a ```plantuml fence should look exactly like a ```css fence — same
punctuation colour, same language-name colour, same block scope — and
the only way to guarantee that is to emit the same scopes;
* the closing-fence rule is stricter than md's parser, which accepts any
indentation and any fence at least as long as the opener (port spec §5,
rule 25). That difference is on purpose. The grammar only paints; the
renderer decides. Matching VS Code here means a fence that looks odd in
the editor looks odd for the same reason every other fence would, and
nobody has to learn a second rule.
The inner `"begin": "(^|\\G)(\\s*)(.*)"` is not a typo and does not
swallow the first line: by the time it is tried, the scanner sits at the
end of the fence line, so `\G` anchors there and `(.*)` matches the empty
remainder. It is a zero-width anchor that hands the following lines to the
embedded grammar. Same trick as markdown-basics.
WHAT IS AND IS NOT HERE
* ```latex and ```tex are md math fences too, but markdown-basics
already injects `text.tex.latex` for both, so only ```math is added.
Adding the other two would mean two grammars racing for the same fence
to no benefit.
* ```mermaid asks for `source.mermaid`, which nothing in a stock VS Code
provides — the built-in mermaid extension ships a renderer, not a
grammar. Same for ```math and `text.tex.latex`, which comes from the
built-in LaTeX extension and can be turned off.
Both therefore carry a second, local pattern beside the include, and
that is NOT belt and braces. Measured against vscode-textmate 9 with
real Oniguruma: when an include naming a grammar that is not installed
is the ONLY pattern of a rule, the rule itself is discarded — not just
the include. The fence then falls through to markdown-basics' unknown-
fence rule and the body loses `meta.embedded.block.mermaid` entirely.
One resolvable sibling pattern keeps the rule alive; the same test
confirms the external grammar still wins every tie when it is present,
because an include contributes its patterns ahead of whatever follows
it. So the local rules are a floor, not a competitor: a couple of
lines of highlighting when nothing better is installed, and invisible
when something is.
* ```csv and ```tsv have no language to embed anywhere, so they are given
a handful of local rules instead. Highlighting numeric cells is not
decoration: md right-aligns exactly those cells in the rendered table
(`isDecimalNumber`), so the colour is a preview of the alignment.
* The ten Graphviz aliases are the ten keys of `graphvizEngines`
(port spec §4 of the HTML-emit spec) and must stay in step with it: a
fence that renders as a diagram but highlights as prose, or the other
way round, is exactly the kind of small lie that costs an afternoon.
There is deliberately no `$schema` key: it makes VS Code fetch a schema
over the network when this file is opened.
The scope name must stay `markdown.md.codeblock` — package.json names it.

md-fenced-plantuml.comment: `plant-uml` is listed first only for readability; Oniguruma backtracks, so alternation order cannot change which alias matches. All three are the aliases md's own code-block dispatch accepts.
md-fenced-plantuml.name: markup.fenced_code.block.markdown

md-fenced-graphviz.comment: The ten `graphvizEngines` keys. `dot` and `gv` and `graphviz` all mean the dot layout; the other seven name a layout engine directly, the way Graphviz itself is invoked.
md-fenced-graphviz.name: markup.fenced_code.block.markdown

md-fenced-mermaid.comment: See the header: `source.mermaid` may not exist, and `#mermaid-minimal` beside it is what keeps the rule — and therefore the embedded scope — alive when it does not.
md-fenced-mermaid.name: markup.fenced_code.block.markdown

md-fenced-math.comment: md renders ```math, ```latex and ```tex identically, as one display formula. Only ```math is claimed here — markdown-basics already owns the other two, with the same `meta.embedded.block.latex` scope, so the three end up looking alike anyway.
md-fenced-math.name: markup.fenced_code.block.markdown

mermaid-minimal.comment: The floor described in the header. Two rules, both of which a real Mermaid grammar would also cover — and would win, since it is included first.

patterns.comment: Mermaid's comment, and its `%%{init: …}%%` directive, which reads as a comment here.
patterns.name: comment.line.percentage.mermaid

latex-minimal.comment: The same floor for ```math. The scopes are the ones the real LaTeX grammar uses for the same things, so on the rare tie this rule wins the colour is still right.

delimited-common.comment: The quoted-field form of RFC 4180, shared by both fences. A doubled quote is the escape, which is why the closing quote carries `(?!\")` — otherwise `"""a"""` closes on the wrong one. md's own `parseDelimited` reads the field exactly this way.

patterns.comment: A whole cell that is a decimal number — the cells md right-aligns. The lookbehind says `nothing, or a comma, immediately before`: `(?<![^,])` is fixed width and so is safe in Oniguruma, where `(?<=^|,)` would not be. Only ASCII space and tab may pad the cell, which is narrower than the parser's whitespace set everywhere else and deliberately so (port spec §5, rule 7): a cell padded with U+200B is not a number on any platform.
patterns.name: constant.numeric.delimited

tsv-cells.comment: Same as `csv-cells`, with the tab as separator. The tab is not scoped: painting an invisible character achieves nothing.
